data.title: Interfaith and Intra-Faith Engagement of the Jacobite Syrian Orthodox Diaspora in Australia
data.abstractNote: The Syriac Orthodox Church of Antioch and all the East is one of the oldest Christian communities. The largest branch of the church is the Jacobite Syrian Orthodox community, located predominantly in the south of India. For political, social, and economic reasons, many of its members are now migrating to countries such as Australia. Like other settler groups, they face acculturation challenges. Members of the Jacobite Syrian Orthodox Church are pursuing strategies to support one another and pass on their traditions intergenerationally while purposefully engaging with the ‘mainstream’ host community in family life, work, and intercultural relationships. Using the lens of Berry’s taxonomy of acculturation, this study draws on in-depth interviews with members of the Jacobite Syrian Orthodox Church in Canberra to assess how they have settled. It contributes to our understanding of what they are bringing to the broader Christian narrative and provides lessons for faith-based communities seeking to engage in meaningful interfaith relationships. My research reveals that shared heritage identity, religious belief and practice, diasporic consciousness, and embracing the host country’s multi-faith multiculturalism are helping Jacobite Syrian Orthodox migrants integrate into Australian society.

data.title: Theodorus van Mopsuestia in het kader van de Syrische dialoog
data.abstractNote: The Third Syriac Consultation of the Syriac Dialogue between the different Churches of the Syriac traditions took place at Mundelein near Chicago, Illinois, in July 1997. One of the main topics of the Consultation concerned the person and the teaching of Theodore of Mopsuestia, who died in 428, before the great Christological controversy between Alexandria and Antioch broke out. Cyril of Alexandria had succeeded in condemning his rival Nestorius at the Council of Ephesus in 431. Soon afterwards Cyril’s supporters in Syria and Egypt started a campaign against the Antiochene ‘forerunners’ of Nestorius. Especially Theodore of Mopsuestia was accused of being the ‘father of Nestorianism’, but Cyril decided not to condemn Theodore officially. In the meantime Theodore’s writings had begun to circulate in Syriac translations in the Church of the East in the Sasanian Empire. It would last until the reign of the Emperor Justinian (527-565) that the issue was reopened. Theodore Askidas, Justinian’s theological advisor, started a deadly attack on Theodore of Mopsuestia who in his eyes should by all means be condemned officially by the Church. Because of the inconsistent attitude of the Roman Pope Vigilius, Justinian convoked a council at Constantinople in 553. The programme of the Council had been carefully drawn up by Askidas and Justinian and the issue of the Council was clear from its start: Theodore of Mopsuestia was to be condemned as the ‘father of Nestorianism’, even given the fact that he had passed away 125 years ago. No real discussion took place about Theodore’s theological background and Theodore’s real vision on the person of Christ. In the Church of the East Theodore lives on as the great ‘interpreter’ of Scripture.

data.abstractNote: "Le problème du Pseudo-Macaire comporte une série de questions assez difficiles à résoudre tant que l'origine et la tradition des homélies messaliennes ne sont pas élucidées; la solution ne peut se trouver que dans les manuscrits ou la découverte éventuelle d'un document. data.title: Sources and Redaction in the Account of the Emperor Julian in Book 3 of Theodoret’s Historia Ecclesiastica
data.abstractNote:
Given the interest in both late antique historiography and the emperor Julian, there is a surprising lack of scholarship concerning the image of Julian presented by Theodoret, the fifth-century bishop of Cyrus, whose Historia ecclesiastica is one of our most important sources of late antique history. This dissertation provides a granular analysis of nineteen episodes dealing with the treatment of the reign of the Emperor Julian in Book 3 of Theodoret’s Historia ecclesiastica. These passages, which account for two-thirds of Book 3, discuss the emperor and his policies in the context of three major themes: Julian’s war on Christianity (Chapter 4), Julian’s interactions with demons and oracles (Chapter 5), and the divine retribution enacted upon Julian and his followers (Chapter 6).
Chapter 4, “War on Christianity,” includes nine episodes: the desecration of the bones of John the Baptist (3.7.1), the persecution of Mark of Arethusa (3.7.6–10), the confession of Theodorus (3.11.1–3), the martyrdom of Juventinus and Maximinus (3.15.1–9), the confession of Valentinian (3.16.1–5), the gold distribution ceremony (3.17.1–8), the martyrdom of the Dux Artemius (3.18.1–2), the defiance of Publia (3.19.1–6), and the speech of the Beroean magistrate (3.22.1–5). Chapter 5, “Demons and Oracles,” includes five episodes: Julian’s initiation in Greece (3.3.1–7), the transfer of Babylas and destruction of the temple of Apollo (3.10.1–3.11.5), the prophecies concerning Julian’s Persian expedition (3.21.1–6), the visions of the pedagogue and monk (21.23–24), and the discovery of the Antiochene skulls and the Carrhaean haruspicy (3.26–27). Chapter 6, “Divine Retribution,” includes four episodes: the punishment of the persecutors of Cyril of Heliopolis (3.7.2–4), the desecrations committed by the Prefect Julian, Felix, and Elpidius (3.12.1–13.4), the attempt to rebuild the Temple of Jerusalem (3.20.1–8), and the death of Julian in Persia (3.25.1–7).
The analysis of each episode begins with a detailed discussion of Theodoret’s sources for that episode followed by a literary and ideological analysis of how Theodoret uses each of those source in his own account. For the episodes for which Theodoret is the only extant source, some attention is given to his possible sources, but the analysis is focused primarily on how the episode illustrates Theodoret’s literary techniques, theological interests, and historiographical methods. Earlier work on Theodoret’s sources identified a number of possible sources for various episodes, but did not demonstrate precisely where and how Theodoret employed them. This study, based on a detailed analysis that compares Theodoret’s text to all relevant parallels, demonstrates the complex way he uses his source material, often weaving together two or more sources into a single narrative.
The results of the source-critical analyses in many cases agree with earlier studies in recognizing Theodoret’s use of Rufinus, the so-called anonymous “Arian Historian,” Gregory of Nazianzus, John Chrysostom, and Antiochene oral tradition. Some earlier studies have also noted a connection between Theodoret and the Historia ecclesiastica of Sozomen, although scholars differ about how to best explain that connection. The analysis undertaken in this study clearly demonstrates a direct literary connection between Theodoret and Sozomen based on evidence that appears in Book 3, although this analysis has found no decisive evidence from which to establish the priority of one author over the other. Nevertheless, this study provides a great deal of data that could help to answer this question if considered together with data from similar analyses of the remaining books in Theodoret’s Historia ecclesiastica. The evidence gathered through this project also supports the common use of the Arian Historian as the simplest way to explain the clear connections between Philostorgius and Theodoret. The careful study of Book 3 also provides substantial evidence that the ninth-century chronicler Theophanes, in addition to using the Arian Historian and the Epitome of Theodorus Anagnostes, may have also used Theodoret's history directly.
The redaction-critical analyses undertaken in this study demonstrate how Theodoret dramatizes his source material with specific language and themes that shape Book 3 into a cohesive narrative depicting Julian as a wicked tyrant whose lust for power drives him to embrace false gods and attempt a war on Christianity on their behalf. Nevertheless, Julian is thwarted by the efforts of bold and pious Christians and finally forced to admit the power of Christ as he is overcome by divine retribution.

data.abstractNote: Before the First World War there were certain differences in cultural and social dimensions between Nestorians and Armenians. In this context Armenians and Nestorians which lived in different areas, disliking each other, they did not intermarry and even did not go to each other’s churches.
